text: The infatuation arrives on schedule: a student, her teacher, the familiar asymmetry. Then it refuses to end when such things are supposed to end. Nils Malmros gives this two full hours, a long time to sit inside one young woman's weather, and the length is doing work; what begins as a romance becomes a question of whether she can still be reached. Kærlighedens smerte came out of Denmark in 1992, and both of the country's film prizes, the Bodil and the Robert, called it the best Danish film of its year. Nothing in it is staged as tragedy. A face, a room, a season passing. The harm accumulates at the speed of ordinary life, which is the speed at which it is hardest to see coming.

A butcher who plays Elvis records loses his pregnant wife to a dentist, and his twelve-year-old son goes with her. Lasse is clever and he is hard, the two qualities least useful in the house he arrives at: authority at the table, a stepsister keeping score, rules where there used to be a shrug. Birger Larsen holds the whole thing to eighty-nine minutes, tight enough that the boy's manoeuvring registers as strategy rather than mood, and the comedy of the setup never quite cancels the arithmetic underneath it. Denmark's two film academies both named it the year's best, and the country sent it forward to the Academy Awards. What it keeps returning to is not whether a child can obey, but what obedience costs when the man demanding it is a stranger.

An eleven-year-old tells a sewer cleaner that she is a Russian princess with Bolsheviks on her trail, and he believes her. Emma has money, an only child's boredom, and parents whose attention is spent elsewhere; the kidnapping she arranges is aimed squarely at them. What she finds instead is Malthe, who works under the street and takes her story at face value because kindness in him runs ahead of judgement. Søren Kragh-Jacobsen puts the two of them in a small room with a large fiction, and the film is funniest exactly where it is most precarious. Both the Bodil and the Robert went to it as the best Danish film of 1988. Ninety-three minutes, most of them belonging to a girl learning what a lie can be asked to carry.

A baptism, a funeral and a wedding, and what the film watches is the hours on either side of each. Carsten Rudolf sets Menneskedyret among provincial Danes obliged to gather three times, dress accordingly and behave, then gives himself seventy-nine minutes to see what leaks out between occasions. A woman carries ambitions that went nowhere. A boy asks the questions the room has agreed not to. The minister is no help, or is help of a kind nobody requested. The vantage is the boy's, but nothing has been scaled down for him: the adults are the subject, and their compromises appear at full size. Ceremony here works less as ritual than as deadline, the day by which everyone must have settled on who they are pretending to be.

The bargain is the whole story: a daughter offered in place of a father, a life inside the castle set against a life outside it. Forty-seven minutes is what this telling has, made for American television in 1983 and drawn rather than photographed, and the brevity need not be a loss, since a tale this familiar can skip its own explanations and go straight to the terms. Drawing also solves the problem that defeats most live versions, a creature who has to be looked at steadily and believed; the line asserts him and the scene proceeds. What remains is the negotiation itself, conducted inside a house one party has promised never to leave, and the odd courtesy such an arrangement demands of both of them.

Two teenagers in a Kansas town are told, by every adult with authority over them, that the one thing they want is the one thing forbidden. The boy's family owns the town, so his appetites will be quietly managed and hers will be publicly judged, and nobody has to say the arrangement aloud. Elia Kazan spends two hours here, much of it on parents talking around the subject in kitchens and parlours, which is where the film keeps its violence. The screenplay won an Academy Award and the picture stands on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest. What is at risk is never really the romance, which is conceded early and by everyone in town. It is a young woman's confidence in her own judgement, taken apart by people convinced they are protecting her.

The man is punctual, courteous and good with figures; murder is simply the line of work he entered after the bank let him go. Charlie Chaplin plays him as a professional with a schedule to keep, and the comedy comes from the logistics rather than the crime: trains to catch, wives to be kept in separate cities, a household budget that all of it quietly serves. There is a wife and a child at home who know nothing, and their comfort is the entire justification, offered without embarrassment. Then two of the widows decline to behave like the others and the routine starts costing him time. The National Board of Review called it the best film of 1947; Cahiers du Cinéma's 100 plus beaux films du monde and TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest have carried it since.

A man who wanted to build things is put on a road crew instead, and the distance between those two facts is one wrongful conviction. He came back from the First World War with plans to become an architect; the economy of 1932 had other uses for him, and then the law found a use of its own. The chain gang is filmed as an economic arrangement rather than a moral one: bodies acquired cheap, guarded, and worked. Mervyn LeRoy takes ninety-two minutes, fast enough that the descent reads less as tragedy than as a series of doors closing at ordinary speed. The National Board of Review named it the best film of 1932, and it later entered the National Film Registry. The picture is set in its own present, which is what gives its plainest scenes their pressure.

Extremadura in the 1960s: a large estate, the families who serve it, and a distance between them that everyone involved has agreed to call natural. The work is the real content, errands and fetching and hours spent waiting to be needed, and Mario Camus stages it without heat, which is what makes the humiliation legible. Paco el Bajo carries orders across the land and hopes, quietly and on little evidence, that his children will be sent to school. That hope is the only future anyone in the frame proposes. Made in 1984 and set two decades earlier, the film has the calm of something recalled rather than argued. Cruelty here is almost never intended. It is simply the shape the arrangement takes when nobody interferes with it.

A telegram arrives at a bad moment and asks a woman to visit the father she has not seen in nine years. Elisa goes; her own marriage is coming apart, which makes the errand easier to accept than to refuse. What follows is largely two people in a house outside Madrid, talking and not talking, a birthday visit that quietly extends itself once the rest of the family drives back to the city. Carlos Saura takes a hundred and twenty-five minutes and very little event, on the wager that a daughter learning why her father left is enough to hold a film. It stands on Caimán's 100 mejores películas del cine español. Explanation, it turns out, is not the same thing as forgiveness, and the film knows the difference.

The plan is a car wash in Pittsburgh, and neither man is anywhere near Pittsburgh. Two drifters fall in together on the road and keep going, and for a hundred and twelve minutes that is nearly the whole of the structure: lifts taken, women visited, towns entered and left, the plan restated aloud as though saying it were a way of saving for it. Jerry Schatzberg is not much interested in incident. He is interested in what two people do with the hours between incidents, which is talk, needle each other, and work out by degrees how much they are willing to be responsible for. Cannes gave it the Palme d'Or in 1973, along with the OCIC prize. The premise offers almost nothing, and the film collects on it slowly.

A week's leave, five prisoners, and a country organised along much the same lines as the prison they came from. Each man travels toward people who have kept accounts in his absence: families with their own sentences to pass, a village with its rules, officials at every stage of the road. The leave turns out to be a change of jurisdiction rather than a release. Yol is filed as a French production and everything inside it is Turkish, a fact that sits in the credits without comment and explains a great deal. Yılmaz Güney directs a hundred and ten minutes largely made of travel: buses, waiting rooms, papers shown on request. It took the Palme d'Or. The men are not being punished in these scenes. They are only going home.

In this house there are two accounts of where the father has gone, and the six-year-old is given only one of them. Malik has no way to test what he is told, so the film settles at roughly his height: weddings, quarrels, meals, the absorbing private business of being small while the adults conduct something else in the next room. Emir Kusturica lets Yugoslavia in the 1950s arrive as a change in how people speak rather than as history, and a hundred and thirty-six minutes is what that method needs, long enough for pressure to register as ordinary family weather. It took the Palme d'Or and the FIPRESCI prize at Cannes. Malik's ignorance is never worked as suspense; it is the condition of childhood in a household that has learned to be careful.

A man loses a finger to a machine and begins, for the first time, doing arithmetic about his own body. The injury does not ennoble him. It makes him available: to political groups, to organisers, to anyone with a use for a worker who has started asking what the work is for, and their plans for him are never quite his own. Elio Petri builds the film out of noise and repetition, a hundred and thirteen minutes shaped like a shift, the same motions and the same clock and the private accounting a man performs while his hands go on without him. It argues rather than illustrates, and it is unkind to nearly everyone in the argument, including the people it agrees with. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix; the David di Donatello named it best film.
